title: Khan Bahadur Khan's Bareilly State
subtitle: The Forgotten Throne of Rohilkhand
region: Bareilly, Rohilkhand and the Nepal frontier
moral: Regional memory can carry a kingdom's unfinished claim.

sources.citation: Trial records of Khan Bahadur Khan Rohilla, India Office Records, IOR/L/MIL/17/5 series
sources.note: Primary evidence for his government, capture and conviction.

sources.citation: G.B. Malleson, History of the Indian Mutiny, vol. 6 (1880); G.W. Forrest, Selections, vol. 3
sources.note: Colonial accounts of Rohilkhand operations and administration.

sources.citation: Khan Bahadur Khan coins, Bareilly mint, 1857-58, described in numismatic catalogues
sources.note: Material evidence of restored sovereignty claims.

panels.shot: epic low-angle wide of a rebel durbar

dialogue.text: In 1857, as empires cracked, Khan Bahadur Khan Rohilla ruled Bareilly with courts, coin and command—yet his rebel state is a throne history almost forgot.
He was Khan Bahadur Khan, grandson of Rohilla chief Hafiz Rahmat Khan—born into a memory of fallen power, raised under the Company that had crushed his house.
Rohilkhand had once been a Rohilla Afghan domain. By 1857 Bareilly was a British district, its Afghan elite watching in silence as foreign rule spread over their land.

dialogue.speaker: khan_bahadur_khan_rohilla
dialogue.text: Our fathers ruled these plains. We live now by their mercy.
When news of Meerut and Delhi reached Bareilly, the storm broke. In May 1857 the sepoys mutinied, British authority collapsed, and the old question returned—who would rule Rohilkhand now?
From June 1857, trial records place Khan Bahadur Khan at the centre. In the vacuum, the Rohilla descendant stepped forward and took charge of Bareilly.
His government shaped itself quickly. Trial evidence and colonial reports describe his courts sitting, petitions heard, disputes settled—Bareilly did not drift, it was ruled.
He collected land revenue, issued orders, tried to keep order on the roads. The records speak of an administration, not merely a riot.
Most telling are the coins. Bareilly’s mint struck pieces in his name in 1857–58—hard metal proof that he claimed restored sovereignty over Rohilkhand.
Yet he saw Bareilly as part of a wider struggle. From his domain he sent the able Bakht Khan to Delhi to lead rebel forces there, tying Rohilkhand to the Mughal centre.

dialogue.speaker: khan_bahadur_khan_rohilla
dialogue.text: Carry our strength to Delhi. Let them know Rohilkhand stands.
Later, sources mention his cooperation with Ahmadullah Shah, the famed fighting maulvi. Rohilkhand’s rebel government linked arms with other centres of resistance.
But as 1857 turned to 1858, British columns pushed back across North India. Malleson and Forrest record their advance toward Rohilkhand, the circle tightening around Bareilly.
The rebel state met organised counter-attack. Operations described in colonial chronicles show Rohilkhand as a theatre of war, not a side note to Delhi.
By May 1858, British control over Bareilly was reasserted. Khan Bahadur Khan’s administration broke; he left the city, beginning a hard flight toward the Nepal frontier.
The India Office trial papers trace his last journey north. The rebel ruler of Bareilly turned fugitive, seeking refuge closer to Nepal as British pursuit spread.
He was captured on that frontier and brought back in chains. His name moved from rebel coin to trial docket, from throne room to courtroom.
The India Office Records preserve his trial—evidence of his rule, his orders, his coins, weighed now as proof of rebellion against the Company’s crown.
From those papers comes his fate. The court condemned him, and the man who had ruled Bareilly as a Rohilla prince was marked for the gallows.
On 24 February 1860, at Bareilly Kotwali, the sentence was carried out. The rebel state of Rohilkhand ended with its ruler’s death in the town he had once governed.
English histories linger on Delhi and Kanpur, yet Bareilly’s records and coins recall a rebel Rohilla state that briefly rose again—and how regional memory can carry a kingdom’s unfinished claim.
